topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: Counting Pi with Bouncing Blocks
target_audience: Advanced High School and Undergraduate Physics/Math Students

outline.topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: Counting Pi with Bouncing Blocks
outline.target_audience: Advanced High School and Undergraduate Physics/Math Students

sections.title: The Setup: The Ant and the Elephant
sections.content: Introduce the physical scenario: A frictionless surface with a vertical wall on the left. We have two blocks: Block A (small mass $m=1$) and Block B (large mass $M$). Block B slides toward the wall, sandwiching Block A in between. We count every collision (Block A hitting the wall or Block A hitting Block B).
sections.example: Visualize a tiny Ant pushing a 1kg sugar cube and a giant Elephant pushing a massive 100kg crate. As the crate moves left, the sugar cube bounces rapidly between the crate and the wall.

sections.title: The Pattern: A Mysterious Number Emerges
sections.content: Observe the total number of collisions as the mass of Block B ($M$) increases by powers of 100 ($M = 100^d$). Show a scoreboard tracking the 'clack' sounds of collisions.
sections.example: If $M=1$, collisions = 3. If $M=100$, collisions = 31. If $M=10,000$, collisions = 314. The digits of $\pi$ (3.14159...) appear as the mass ratio grows!

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: To solve this, we need two laws: 1. Conservation of Energy (Elastic collisions keep the 'total speed' constant in a specific way). 2. Conservation of Momentum. Graphically, the energy equation $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}MV^2 = E$ represents an ellipse in the velocity phase space ($v, V$).
sections.example: Imagine a coordinate system where the x-axis is the small block's velocity and the y-axis is the large block's velocity. We rescale the axes so the ellipse becomes a perfect circle.

sections.title: The Geometric Twist: Collisions as Rotations
sections.content: In our 'Circle Phase Space,' every collision between blocks corresponds to a reflection across a line, and every wall hit corresponds to a reflection across the axis. Two reflections equal one rotation by a fixed angle $\theta$.
sections.example: Animate a point 'jumping' around the perimeter of a circle. Each jump is a collision. The total number of jumps is how many times the angle $\theta$ fits into the total arc of the circle.

sections.title: The Mathematical Bridge: Small Angles and Pi
sections.content: As the mass $M$ gets larger, the rotation angle $\theta$ becomes very small. Specifically, $\theta \approx \sqrt{m/M}$. The total angle of the 'journey' in phase space is $\pi$ radians. The number of collisions $N$ is roughly $\pi / \theta$.
sections.example: Show the calculation: If $M=100$, $\theta \approx 0.1$. $\pi / 0.1 \approx 31.4$. Since we can't have half a collision, we get 31. This matches our observation perfectly!

sections.title: Summary: The World's Most Inefficient Calculator
sections.content: Recap how kinetic energy geometry links to the most famous constant in circles. While beautiful, it's the 'slowest' way to calculate $\pi$ because for 10 digits, you need a mass ratio of $100^9$!
sections.example: A final animation shows the Elephant's crate becoming a mountain-sized block, the collisions sounding like a machine gun, and the scoreboard displaying 3.14159265...

storyboard.title: The Setup: The Ant and the Elephant
lecture_lines: Imagine two blocks on a frictionless floor.
Small block sits between a wall and large block.
We count every collision until the blocks separate.
animations: Draw white #FFFFFF wall on left and green #00FF00 ground line.
Place small blue #0000FF Block A and large red #FF0000 Block B.
Animate Block B sliding left at constant velocity towards Block A.
Flash Block A yellow #FFFF00 when it hits the wall or Block B.
Show 'Total Collisions: 0' text at top center in white #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: The Pattern: A Mysterious Number Emerges
lecture_lines: Let the large block move toward the wall.
If masses are equal, we count three collisions.
Increase the large mass by factors of one hundred.
The collision counts remarkably reveal digits of pi.
Why does this physical system calculate pi?
animations: Set M=100; Block A bounces rapidly between wall and Block B.
Increment scoreboard from 0 up to 31 with each contact.
Highlight the final '31' in yellow #FFFF00 once movement stops.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Kinetic energy conservation defines an elliptical velocity relationship.
Momentum conservation governs how velocities change during collisions.
We rescale the velocity axes to simplify the ellipse.
Rescaling transforms the energy ellipse into a perfect circle.
Now, every state becomes a point on this circle.
animations: Display energy conservation formula 0.5mv^2 + 0.5MV^2 = E in white #FFFFFF.
Draw a red #FF0000 ellipse on a velocity coordinate plane.
Smoothly transform the red ellipse into a white #FFFFFF circle.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Twist: Collisions as Rotations
lecture_lines: Each collision maps to a reflection in phase space.
Two reflections combine to form a single rotation.
The rotation angle depends on the mass ratio.
Every "clack" is a jump around the circle's perimeter.
The total journey spans exactly pi radians.
animations: Place a point P on the circle perimeter to represent state.
Reflect P across y-axis for wall collision, then slanted line for block collision.
Label the resulting rotation as angle theta in orange #FFA500.
Show multiple jumps of P tracing the circle arc.
Highlight the total angular distance covered as Pi radians.

storyboard.title: The Mathematical Bridge: Small Angles and Pi
lecture_lines: For large masses, the rotation angle becomes very small.
The number of collisions is pi divided by the angle.
This explains why the digits of pi appear.
animations: Show formula theta approx sqrt(m/M) in light blue #ADD8E6.
Overlay 'N = Pi / theta' text near the circle arc.
Show result N = 314 for M = 10,000 in white #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Summary: The World's Most Inefficient Calculator
lecture_lines: Geometry links billiard ball physics to circular constants.
It is a beautiful but inefficient way to calculate pi.
One hundred billion kilograms yields only six digits.
animations: Final scene: massive Block B causes rapid-fire collisions.
Scoreboard counts rapidly to 3.14159265... in gold #FFD700.
Fade out blocks and wall, leaving only the digits of Pi.
